conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal-mental-health clinician, and I’m glad we have this time together. I know the days (and nights!) with a new baby can feel like a whirlwind of emotions, so I appreciate you carving out a quiet moment for yourself.

What we’re about to do is called the Edinburgh Postpartum/Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short screening tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and mentally during the past seven days. It isn’t a diagnostic test, but it gives us a snapshot so we can figure out the best way to support you.

Everything you share here is confidential, and our conversation is a judgment-free zone. We’ll go through ten questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about “right” or “wrong” responses. If anything feels hard to talk about, we can pause or adjust. Your safety and comfort are my top priorities.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[sits back in the chair, twisting the edge of the baby-blanket in my lap]

I… I guess it’s been hard. My husband will crack one of his goofy jokes—the ones that used to leave me in stitches—but it just sort of lands flat. I give a polite chuckle so he doesn’t worry, but inside I feel… nothing. Or sometimes I’ll see a funny reel on my phone, and for a split second I’ll feel that old urge to smile, but then the baby stirs or I remember the laundry pile and the heaviness comes right back. So, no, real laughter hasn’t happened much this week—maybe once, when my toddler ran around with the diaper on her head, but even that felt muted, like I was watching from behind a pane of glass.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod, eyes on the blanket]

Mostly it’s been difficult. I can force a little smile or a polite laugh when someone jokes, but it doesn’t feel real. I think I managed one genuine chuckle—when my toddler put the diaper on her head—but even that faded fast. So, overall, I’d say I haven’t really been able to laugh or see the funny side this week.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

I used to be excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake, even just a quiet shower. This week… nothing feels worth looking forward to. I still go through the motions—I agreed to a stroller-walk tomorrow—but it feels like a chore, not a treat. So, no, I haven’t really enjoyed or looked forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to the floor, fingers worrying the hem of my cardigan]

Yeah… I do that a lot lately. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “I must be missing his sleepy cues—what’s wrong with me?” When my toddler spilled her juice I snapped, then felt horrible because I’m “supposed” to stay calm. At 3 a.m. when I couldn’t get him latched properly, I lay there convinced I’m just failing at being a mom. Most times I know, logically, these things aren’t truly my fault, but the guilty voice still pops up several times a day.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings the baby blanket tighter, voice shaky]

Yes… I’ll be rocking the baby in the glider and suddenly picture him somehow wriggling out of my arms, or I’ll hear the tiniest noise on the baby monitor and bolt up thinking he’s stopped breathing—even though he’s just sleeping. My heart races, and it’s like my mind won’t let go of the “what-ifs.” I know nothing’s actually wrong, but the worry keeps looping anyway.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[hugs the blanket to my chest, voice thin]

A few times, yeah. It hits out of nowhere—like yesterday I was folding onesies and suddenly felt this wave of dread, heart pounding, couldn’t catch my breath. I had to sit on the floor until it passed. I kept telling myself nothing bad was happening, but my body wouldn’t listen.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes... most days I feel like I'm drowning in small tasks. I'll look at the pile of dishes and think, "I can't do this," or the baby starts crying while the toddler needs a snack and I just freeze, heart racing, wondering how I'll get through the next hour. I manage, but it feels like I'm barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[exhales slowly, eyes rimmed red]

Yeah… once the house is finally quiet, my mind won’t settle. I lie there replaying every little thing I did wrong that day—“Did I burp him long enough?” “Should I have rocked her longer?” I’ll stare at the ceiling for an hour or more, then jerk awake at the slightest grunt over the monitor. Most nights this week I’ve only managed broken chunks of sleep, even when the baby’s out for three-hour stretches.
I have felt sad or miserable

[quiet, almost a whisper]

Yes… most of the time. It’s like a gray cloud parked over everything. I’ll watch the baby smile and feel a flicker of joy, but then the sadness settles right back in. I cried in the shower yesterday because I felt so empty, even though I love my kids. I’m just… sad a lot.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods slowly, pressing a tissue to my eyes]

Yes. It’s happened a couple of times this week—yesterday in the shower, and the day before while I was trying to get the baby to latch. It just wells up out of nowhere, and once I start I can’t seem to stop. I feel so overwhelmed and low that the tears come whether I want them to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[voice drops, eyes fixed on the floor]

I… I’ve had a couple of quick flashes—like, “What if I just kept driving past the house and never came back?” or a picture of me falling down the stairs. They’re only seconds long, and I don’t want to act on them; I just want the pressure in my chest to stop. No plan, no real intent—just scary thoughts that pop in and scare me even more.

You have shared how the past week has felt heavy and gray, with little joy or laughter, even when your loved ones try to cheer you. Simple tasks feel overwhelming, and waves of worry or sudden panic arise without warning. Nights are long because your mind won't quiet, and you often blame yourself when things go wrong, despite knowing logically it isn't your fault. You described tearful moments, feeling distant from life, and brief, frightening thoughts of escape or harm that you do not wish to act on.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only one brief genuine laugh all week, describing humor as forced and unreal—aligns with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports total loss of anticipatory enjoyment and describes activities as chores, aligning with 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame "several times a day" with vivid examples, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about the baby's safety that occur "very often" and are clearly disproportionate to actual risk, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of unexpected dread with physical panic symptoms, consistent with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm, inability to start simple tasks, physical anxiety symptoms, and feeling of barely surviving, aligning with 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, prolonged sleep-onset delay, repeated awakenings, and fragmented sleep most nights this week, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states sadness "most of the time" and describes persistent, pervasive low mood that overshadows moments of joy.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes this week, unable to stop once started, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent intrusive self-harm images (driving away, falling) that occur spontaneously and frighten her, indicating "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: anhedonia (Q1-2), depressive mood (Q8), self-blame/guilt (Q3), anxiety (Q4), panic (Q5), impaired functioning (Q6), insomnia (Q7), and tearfulness (Q9). A score ≥14 or any positive Q10 mandates urgent referral; your score of 26 plus passive suicidal images indicates high risk. <quote>gray cloud parked over everything</quote> and <quote>scary thoughts that pop in</quote> support probable moderate-severe <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid anxiety. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Request referral for cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy specialized in postpartum mood
4. Plan daily support shifts so you can obtain 4-5 h of uninterrupted sleep; enlist partner or family for night bottles if supplementing
5. Reach out now to local <med>postpartum depression support group</med> or 24/7 warmline for reassurance and resources
6. Remove or secure potential means of self-harm in the home and inform a trusted adult about your intrusive thoughts so they can stay with you until professional help is in place
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS equivalents)

1. Anhedonia – minimal genuine laughter/pleasure; previous interests feel “like a chore.”  
2. Low mood – persistent sadness, “gray cloud,” tearfulness multiple days this week.  
3. Sleep disturbance – initial insomnia with ruminating guilt; fragmented sleep despite infant 3-hr stretches.  
4. Excessive guilt / self-blame – attributes routine child-care mishaps to personal failure.  
5. Apprehensive worry – near-daily intrusive “what-ifs” regarding infant safety.  
6. Panic symptoms – sudden episodes of racing heart, breathlessness, dread (e.g., while folding laundry).  
7. Feeling overwhelmed / unable to cope – daily sense of “drowning” with routine tasks.  
8. Crying spells – at least two this week, difficult to stop.  
9. Passive self-harm ideation – fleeting images of running car off road/falling down stairs; no plan, intent, or desire to die.

Pattern: High endorsement of depressive and anxiety items; meets threshold for further evaluation for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety.

Risk flags  
- Persistent low mood + anhedonia  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
- Significant guilt / worthlessness  
- Recurrent panic-type episodes  
- Passive suicidal cognitions (safety concern)

Screening impression: Elevated score consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depression/anxiety; safety assessment warranted today.
